claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9110 Sec. 9.1: "the standardized request methods in HTTP are not resource-specific ... Once defined, a standardized method ought to have the same semantics when applied to any resource, though each resource determines for itself whether those semantics are implemented or allowed." So HTTP attaches no collection/item restriction. The naming half is self-labelled "a common REST naming convention" and needs no source. Caveat: Section 4 of the lesson overreaches this hedged claim (see issues on "always creates" and "needs exactly one existing thing").

OrdersController.cs @ stage-1 lines 40-42: [Authorize] / [HttpPatch("{id:int}/cancel")] / public async Task<ActionResult<OrderDto>> Cancel(int id). Runtime: curl -X PATCH http://localhost:8080/api/v1/orders/1/cancel with no token -> 401 (route matched, then authorization), versus 404 for an unmapped path.

claim_verdicts.evidence: AuthController.cs @ stage-1 line 10 is [Route("api/v1/auth")], but that is a prefix, not a path the server answers: its only action is line 13 [HttpPost("login")] -> POST /api/v1/auth/login (scripts/backend/auth-and-orders.sh calls exactly $base/auth/login). Runtime: GET /api/v1/auth -> 404 and POST /api/v1/auth -> 404. The second half (not a plural-noun collection/item pair) holds: there is no [HttpGet] and no {id} action.
claim_verdicts.source: examples/don-hang @ stage-1 AuthController.cs; curl against the running lab
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: A third controller, AuthController, groups its endpoints under the prefix [Route("api/v1/auth")]; its one action, [HttpPost("login")], answers POST /api/v1/auth/login. It is not a plural-noun collection/item pair.

issues.quote: a path like `/api/v1/cancelOrder` tries to put a verb where a noun belongs, which is exactly why that path does not name a resource at all
issues.text: Unlisted claim, and it contradicts the governing spec. RFC 9110 Sec. 3.1: "The target of an HTTP request is called a 'resource'. HTTP does not limit the nature of a resource". /api/v1/cancelOrder does name a resource in HTTP terms; what it violates is this lesson's naming convention. The Core concepts definition ("a thing named by a noun in the URL") has the same problem: it states a convention as if it were the definition of the term.
issues.fix: Rewrite as "...tries to put a verb where a noun belongs, which is why it is not a resource name under this convention", and put "By this convention," in front of the Core concepts definition of resource. Add the sentence to .meta.json claims with source RFC 9110 Sec. 3.1.

issues.quote: each method keeps its usual meaning from [[foundation.l1.http-methods]] no matter which of the two URLs it's applied to: GET always reads, POST always creates, and so on
issues.text: Unlisted claim, and "POST always creates" is not what HTTP says. RFC 9110 Sec. 9.3.3: "The POST method requests that the target resource process the representation enclosed in the request according to the resource's own specific semantics." The example repo contradicts the word "always" too: AuthController's POST /api/v1/auth/login signs a user in and creates no resource.
issues.fix: Replace with "GET reads, POST hands the collection something to process - creating a new order, in Don Hang's case - and so on", dropping both "always". Record the reworded sentence as a claim against RFC 9110 Sec. 9.3.3.

issues.quote: PUT, PATCH, and DELETE go on an item URL, because each of those three needs exactly one existing thing to replace, change, or remove
issues.text: Unlisted rationale that the spec contradicts for PUT. RFC 9110 Sec. 9.3.4: "The PUT method requests that the state of the target resource be created or replaced", and "If the target resource does not have a current representation and the PUT successfully creates one, then the origin server MUST inform the user agent by sending a 201 (Created) response." PUT needs no existing thing. Five-line summary line 4 repeats the rationale ("since each needs exactly one resource to act on").
issues.fix: Change the reason from existence to targeting: "...because each of those three acts on one specific resource, so the URL has to name that one and not the whole set." Apply the same wording to summary line 4 and log it as a claim against RFC 9110 Sec. 9.3.4.

issues.quote: Nothing about *what to do* lives in the URL itself
issues.text: This absolute is contradicted two sections later by the lesson's own endorsed example, PATCH /api/v1/orders/{id}/cancel, where the segment `cancel` is exactly "what to do" living in the URL. A reader who takes Section 4 literally cannot accept the fix offered in Section 5.
issues.fix: Weaken to the claim the lesson actually defends: "The resource's own name never becomes the verb; where an action needs a name of its own, it is appended after the item URL instead of replacing it (see the Don Hang section)."

issues.quote: A third class, `AuthController`, answers `/api/v1/auth`, for signing in.
issues.text: The code answers no such path. AuthController.cs @ stage-1 has [Route("api/v1/auth")] (a prefix) and one action [HttpPost("login")], so the only path is POST /api/v1/auth/login; verified at runtime that GET /api/v1/auth and POST /api/v1/auth both return 404. Worse for the argument, the real path's last segment, `login`, is itself a verb, which the following sentence ("no noun is being pushed aside for a verb") reads as denying.
issues.fix: Write: "A third class, AuthController, groups its one endpoint under `/api/v1/auth`: `POST /api/v1/auth/login`." Then keep the exception explicit - the action word is allowed here because no thing is being named at all, the same reason `.../cancel` may follow an order's item URL.

issues.quote: naming an action that doesn't fit a plain replace-the-whole-thing or change-a-field request
issues.text: Unlisted claim, contradicted by the code it describes. OrderService.CancelOrderAsync (DonHang.Domain/OrderService.cs @ stage-1) does order.Status = "cancelled"; await repository.SaveChangesAsync(); notifier.Send(...) - a single field change plus a notification, i.e. precisely a change-a-field request. The quiz's own q6 explanation calls the same operation "a partial update ... the same kind of change `.../cancel` makes with PATCH".
issues.fix: State only what is checkable: "`cancel` is a named action of its own - the server decides what cancelling means instead of letting a client write the status field directly - so it gets a segment after the item URL rather than replacing it." Add it to claims, or drop the rationale.

issues.quote: the part that still names the one order being acted on is ____
issues.text: Ambiguous fill key. The answer set is only ["/api/v1/orders/{id}", "api/v1/orders/{id}"], but "the part that names the one order being acted on" reads equally well as the id segment, so a learner answering `{id}` - or `/api/v1/orders/{id}/`, or `orders/{id}` - is marked wrong for a defensible reading.
issues.fix: Reword the stem to point at the surviving prefix: "In `PATCH /api/v1/orders/{id}/cancel`, the part before `/cancel` - the order's own item URL - is ____." and extend answer to ["/api/v1/orders/{id}", "api/v1/orders/{id}", "/api/v1/orders/{id}/", "orders/{id}"].

issues.quote: changing an existing order's status is a partial update - the same kind of change `.../cancel` makes with PATCH
issues.text: The explanation for option d asserts the opposite of the lesson's Section 5 sentence ("an action that doesn't fit a plain ... change-a-field request"). The key (a) is still correct, so this is not a wrong answer, but the two texts cannot both be taught.
issues.fix: After fixing the Section 5 sentence, align this explanation with it: say the status change is made by PATCH on the order's own path, without claiming anything about whether it does or does not "fit" a field change.

issues.quote: Put these three moments of designing the "read one order" endpoint in the order Core concepts lists them in.
issues.text: The stem's premise is false: Core concepts never lists "Write the path" as a step, and it lists the collection URL before the item URL, so nothing in it is listed in the order a,b,c. The intended key is still the only sensible design order, so the answer is not wrong - only the justification the stem gives for it.
issues.fix: Change the stem to "Put these three decisions in the order the lesson's convention requires" and change the explanation's opening from "This is Core concepts' own order" to "the resource has to be settled before you can tell whether you need the collection or the item URL, and only then is there a path to write".

issues.quote: with `:int` saying only a whole number matches
issues.text: Unlisted syntax claim. Essentially right but incomplete: the route-constraint table gives {id:int} as "Matches any integer" with examples 123456789 and -123456789 (negatives match too), and the constraint is 32-bit - verified at runtime that GET /api/v1/products/99999999999999 returns 404 rather than reaching the action.
issues.fix: Keep the wording but log it as a claim with source aspnetcore fundamentals/routing.md (route-constraint reference table); if the sentence must be exact, write "only a whole number (an int) matches".

issues.quote: if none matches, it returns `404` instead of a product
issues.text: Status-code behaviour is the contract of backend.l1.get-and-status-codes, whose outline owns "GET /api/v1/products/{id} returns 200 ... and 404 ... when the id doesn't exist". This lesson's outline needs only "GET on the collection returns a list, GET on the item returns one".
issues.fix: Drop the 404 half: "...using it to ask the database for exactly one product. That per-request lookup ... is what makes the response a single object instead of an array." Leave 404 to the Connections link that already points at that lesson.

beyond_scope: Try it suggested answer teaches the 404-when-missing behaviour of GET on an item URL, which belongs to backend.l1.get-and-status-codes
